Historical SASRec evaluation differs materially from this benchmark: its reference code samples 100 negatives without deduplicating draws or explicitly excluding the positive, then ranks using double argsort. Preserve the pinned RecHarness protocol—99 unique negatives, fixed users/candidates, seed 42—and reuse identical candidates for original-versus-shuffled comparisons. Sampled HR@10 depends on candidate construction; research finds sampled evaluation can produce different model rankings from full-catalog evaluation. [Reference implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kang205/SASRec/master/util.py), [sampling study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13045).

A random permutation need not change the observed history: duplicate items can exchange positions invisibly, and identity permutations are possible. Consequently, unchanged scores alone do not demonstrate order insensitivity. Diagnostic recommendation: shuffle only nonpadding positions; report the fraction of histories whose item sequences actually changed, and measure score/rank changes separately on those histories. Preserve duplicates and left padding. NumPy documents permutation as shuffling array elements; the duplicate-history implication follows mathematically. [NumPy permutation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/generated/numpy.random.Generator.permutation.html).

Tied scores require explicit interpretation: PyTorch’s stable argsort preserves input order among equal values, so positive-first candidate ordering can favor positives under stable descending sorting. For diagnostics, document the tie rule, measure ties around rank 10, and distinguish numerical score changes from tie-driven rank changes; do not modify the host evaluator. Use evaluation mode and fixed diagnostic randomness so dropout or resampling does not masquerade as sequence sensitivity. [PyTorch argsort](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.argsort.html).
